10390: A marshal is a person in a position of authority whose role is to manage, control, direct, or maintain order — whether in the military, in law enforcement, in a courtroom, or at an event. The word covers quite different roles depending on context, but this idea of organized authority and oversight runs through all of them.

In many countries, a marshal (or field marshal) is the highest possible military rank — above generals, above admirals. It is not a job you work your way into through a normal promotion ladder; it is usually awarded only to commanders of exceptional distinction, often after a major war victory.

  • In the United Kingdom, "Field Marshal" is the top rank of the British Army.
  • In France and historically in many European armies, "Marshal of France" was the supreme military title.
  • In the United States Army, the equivalent is "General of the Army" (five stars), and the rank of marshal does not officially exist — though the spirit is the same.

Think of it this way: if a general commands an army, a marshal commands the generals.
2. A Law Enforcement Officer (Especially in the United States)

In the American legal and governmental system, a marshal is a federal law enforcement officer. This is different from a police officer (who works for a city) or a sheriff (who works for a county). A marshal works for the federal government.

U.S. Marshals are among the oldest law enforcement officers in the country. Their responsibilities include:

  • Enforcing orders issued by federal courts
  • Transporting and guarding federal prisoners
  • Protecting federal judges and witnesses
  • Tracking down federal fugitives

You may also know the word from Old West history and movies, where the town marshal was the local law-enforcement figure — the person responsible for keeping order in a frontier town. This was a more informal, community-level role compared to today's federal marshals, but the idea of legal authority and peacekeeping remains the same.

A court marshal (also called a marshal of the court) is an officer specifically attached to a court of law. They maintain order inside the courtroom, execute the court's instructions, serve legal documents, and ensure proceedings run smoothly.

A marshal in this sense is a person assigned to supervise, direct, or control people and activities at a public event or ceremony. This is probably the broadest everyday use of the word.

Examples:

  • At a parade, marshals guide the procession, manage the crowd, and keep things moving in an orderly way. The lead person at the front is often called the Grand Marshal — an honorary title given to a distinguished person who leads the parade.
  • At a motor race (like Formula 1), track marshals are stationed around the circuit. They wave colored flags to communicate with drivers (yellow for danger, red to stop the race), help recover crashed cars, and assist in emergencies.
  • At a marathon or road race, marshals stand at junctions and turning points to direct runners and keep spectators off the course.
  • At a fire scene, a fire marshal is an official who investigates the cause of a fire, enforces fire-safety regulations, and ensures buildings comply with fire codes.

The common thread here: a marshal at an event is someone with a clearly defined patch of responsibility — they don't just watch, they manage.

An air marshal is an undercover law enforcement officer who travels on commercial passenger flights, disguised as an ordinary traveler. Their purpose is to prevent — or respond to — hijackings, terrorism, or serious threats aboard the aircraft. They carry a weapon and have the authority to act when a flight is in danger. Because they work in secret, you would never know one was on your flight.

Every use of the word "marshal" — no matter the context — shares a common thread:

A marshal is someone invested with formal authority to maintain order, direct operations, or enforce rules within a specific domain.

Whether that domain is a battlefield, a federal courtroom, a race track, or a passenger airplane, the marshal is the person in charge of making sure things go right within their assigned area. The scale and nature of the power varies enormously — from the highest military rank on earth to someone waving a flag at a local fun run — but the essence is always the same: authority plus responsibility for order.
10391:
To marshal something means to carefully gather, organize, or arrange things — or people — in a deliberate, purposeful, and orderly way, usually in preparation for something important.

The key feeling behind this word is intentionality with authority. You are not just casually collecting things or loosely putting them together. You are taking active, deliberate control over scattered elements and bringing them into an ordered form so they are ready for use or action.

1. Marshaling things (ideas, resources, evidence, arguments)

This is the most common use. When you marshal things like thoughts, facts, arguments, or resources, you are pulling them all together and arranging them in a clear, logical, and powerful way — usually because you are about to make a point, fight a battle (literal or figurative), or accomplish a goal.

Examples:

  • "Before the courtroom debate, the lawyer spent hours marshaling her evidence so that each piece would land at exactly the right moment."

Here, she is not just collecting evidence — she is organizing it strategically, deciding what goes first, what supports what, and how it all fits together to build the strongest possible case.

  • "He took a deep breath and marshaled his thoughts before responding to the difficult question."

He is gathering his scattered thinking, bringing order to it, so he can speak clearly and effectively.

  • "The government marshaled enormous resources to respond to the earthquake."

This means the government deliberately pulled together money, people, equipment, and infrastructure — organizing all of it in a coordinated way — for a specific purpose.

Notice the pattern: marshaling = gathering + organizing + purposeful readiness.

2. Marshaling people (guiding or directing them)

In this use, to marshal people means to guide, direct, or lead them in an orderly, controlled way — often with an air of quiet authority — to where they need to go or into some kind of order.

Examples:

  • "The event staff carefully marshaled the crowd through the exits after the concert."

They didn't just open the doors and let chaos happen. They guided people in an organized, orderly manner.

  • "The teacher marshaled the children into two neat lines before the fire drill."

She directed and arranged them deliberately and with calm authority.

This use carries a sense of someone taking charge and bringing order to a group of people who would otherwise be scattered or disorganized.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

"Marshal" is a serious, somewhat formal word. It carries a sense of effort, care, and authority. You would not say "I marshaled my grocery list." That would feel out of place because a grocery list requires no real effort or authority to organize.

You use "marshal" when the stakes feel higher, when the organizing takes real effort or skill, or when the result of that organizing truly matters — a speech, a battle, a crisis response, a legal argument, a crowd of people.

Think of it this way: you organize your bookshelf, but you marshal your forces.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Gather simply means to bring things together in one place. No implication of order or purpose. "She gathered her books."

Organize means to arrange things in a system. It is close to marshal, but it lacks the sense of urgency, authority, and preparation-for-action. "He organized his files."

Assemble means to bring parts or people together into one place. It doesn't carry the strategic or purposeful edge. "They assembled in the hall."

Marshal = gather + organize + arrange with purpose + a sense of authority and readiness for something important. It contains all of these ideas at once, which is why it is the most powerful among them.
To marshal something is to deliberately gather scattered things (or people), bring them under your control, and arrange them in an ordered, purposeful way so they are ready for effective action.
10392: A marsupial is a type of mammal — a warm-blooded animal with a backbone that breathes air, has hair or fur on its body, and feeds its young with milk. But what sets marsupials apart from most other mammals is one remarkable thing: the mother gives birth to her young at an extremely early, underdeveloped stage, and the baby continues growing outside the womb — usually inside a pouch on the mother's body.
The Core Idea: Born Too Early, Grows in a Pouch

In most mammals (like humans, dogs, or elephants), the baby develops fully inside the mother's womb before being born. The baby is relatively well-formed at birth. Marsupials are fundamentally different.

When a marsupial gives birth, the newborn — called a joey — is incredibly tiny and unfinished. It looks almost like a pink, hairless, jellybean-sized creature. Its back legs may barely exist yet. Its eyes and ears are sealed shut. Its organs are still forming. In almost every way, it is not ready for the outside world.

But here is the remarkable part: as soon as the joey is born, it instinctively crawls — using its tiny front legs — through its mother's fur and into her pouch (a fold of skin on her belly). Inside the pouch, it latches onto a nipple and starts drinking milk. It stays there for weeks or even months, continuing the development that other mammals complete inside the womb. The pouch is, in effect, an external womb.

Not all marsupial pouches are the same. Some open at the top (facing upward), like in kangaroos. Some open at the bottom or to the side, like in wombats and koalas. A few marsupials don't even have a true pouch — just a fold of skin that partially covers the joey while it clings to a nipple.

The pouch provides warmth, protection, and a constant food supply. As the joey grows, it eventually becomes strong enough to peek out of the pouch, then to climb in and out on its own, and finally to leave the pouch entirely — though it may return to the pouch for safety for some time after that.

The most well-known marsupials include:

  • Kangaroos — the large, hopping animals native to Australia, famous for carrying their joeys in their forward-facing pouches.
  • Koalas — tree-dwelling animals that eat eucalyptus leaves; their pouch opens at the bottom.
  • Wombats — stocky, burrowing animals; their pouch also opens downward (so soil doesn't enter when they dig).
  • Opossums — the only marsupials native to North America; they are well-known for "playing dead" when threatened.
  • Tasmanian devils — carnivorous marsupials from Tasmania (an island off Australia), known for their powerful jaws and loud screeching.
  • Wallabies — similar to kangaroos but smaller.
  • Quolls — small, spotted, cat-sized carnivores found in Australia and New Guinea.
  • Bandicoots — small, rat-like marsupials that are good at digging.
How Marsupials Differ from Other Mammals

All mammals fall into three broad groups:

  1. Monotremes — the most unusual mammals; they actually lay eggs. Examples: the platypus and echidna.
  2. Marsupials — give birth very early; young develop in a pouch.
  3. Placental mammals — the largest group; the baby develops fully inside the womb through an organ called the placenta. This group includes humans, dogs, cats, horses, whales, bats, and most other mammals you know.

Marsupials do have a very basic, short-lived version of the placenta, but it is far simpler than in placental mammals and doesn't support long-term development inside the womb. This is why marsupials give birth so early.

The vast majority of marsupials — around 70% of all species — are found in Australia, New Guinea, and nearby islands. This is why Australia is so closely associated with them. Australia was isolated from other landmasses for tens of millions of years, which allowed marsupials to evolve and thrive there without much competition from placental mammals.

The Americas (particularly South America) have a smaller but significant group of marsupials, including opossums. In fact, the opossum family is the most species-rich marsupial family in the Americas.

There are no native marsupials in Europe, Asia, or Africa.

There are roughly 330 to 380 known species of marsupials. They come in a wide variety of shapes and lifestyles — some hop, some climb trees, some burrow underground, some swim, and some are fierce predators. Despite their differences, they are all united by that single defining trait: their young are born early and complete their development outside the womb, almost always in a pouch.

A marsupial is a mammal that gives birth to extremely underdeveloped young, which then crawl into the mother's pouch and continue growing there, nourished by her milk. The pouch substitutes for what a womb does in other mammals. Kangaroos, koalas, wombats, and opossums are all marsupials. They are most commonly found in Australia and the Americas, and they form one of the three major groups of living mammals.
10393:
Martial means relating to war, soldiers, combat, or the military. When you call something "martial," you are saying it belongs to the world of fighting, armies, and warfare — or that it carries the spirit of that world.

Think of it this way: if something feels like it belongs on a battlefield, in a military camp, or in the hands of a warrior, the word martial likely fits.

The word works on two levels, and understanding both is key.

1. The Literal Layer — Directly about war and the military

This is the straightforward use. Something is martial if it is actually part of military life or warfare.

  • A martial society is one built around war and armies — like ancient Sparta, where every citizen was trained to fight from childhood.
  • A martial tradition refers to a culture's long history of warfare and soldiering.
  • A martial code is a set of rules and values that soldiers live by — things like honour, discipline, and obedience.

2. The Descriptive Layer — Feels like war or a soldier

Here, "martial" is used more broadly to describe things that suggest or evoke the energy of war — even if no actual war is happening.

  • A person with a martial bearing stands very straight, moves with precision, and has the disciplined posture of a soldier.
  • A martial tone in someone's speech is firm, commanding, and forceful — like an officer giving orders.
  • Martial music is bold, loud, and stirring — the kind that makes you feel like marching or going into battle. Think of drums and brass instruments playing a powerful rhythm.

These are the combinations you will encounter most often in life. Knowing them will serve you extremely well.

Martial arts
This is probably the most common use you already know. Martial arts are fighting techniques and combat systems — such as karate, judo, kung fu, taekwondo, and boxing. The word "arts" here means skills or disciplines. So "martial arts" literally means combat skills. Notice how "martial" frames these as fighting-based disciplines, not just sports.

Martial law
This is when a government hands control of a country — or a city or region — over to the military, suspending normal civilian laws and courts. It is usually declared in times of extreme crisis: a coup, a war, a massive civil breakdown. Under martial law, soldiers police the streets, curfews are enforced, and regular civil rights may be suspended. The phrase captures the idea that the law itself has become military.

Court martial (also written court-martial)
This is a military court — a special legal trial held within the armed forces to judge soldiers accused of breaking military rules or laws. Ordinary citizens go to civilian courts; soldiers can be taken before a court martial. The word is also used as a verb: "He was court-martialled for desertion."

Martial spirit
This phrase describes a mindset — a person's inner drive to fight, compete, and conquer. It doesn't require an actual war. An athlete with a strong martial spirit is fiercely competitive, determined, and refuses to give up. It's the warrior's attitude applied to any challenge.

"Martial" is not a neutral word. It carries weight and seriousness. It suggests:

  • Discipline — the rigid, trained self-control of a soldier
  • Aggression — the willingness to fight and dominate
  • Power — physical or institutional strength
  • Order — military precision and structure

Because of this, writers and speakers use "martial" intentionally when they want to signal that something is serious, forceful, and combat-related — whether literally or in spirit.
How It Differs From Similar Words

It helps to see how "martial" sits alongside related words:

  • Military is a broader, more general word simply meaning "of the army/armed forces." Martial is more intense and evocative — it specifically pulls in the fighting, warlike spirit of the military, not just its bureaucratic or organizational side.
  • Warlike is the closest plain-English synonym, but it sounds more informal and less precise.
  • Belligerent means actively aggressive and looking for a fight — this focuses on attitude. Martial focuses more on belonging to the world of combat.
  • Aggressive is about personality and behaviour. Martial is about identity and domain — it describes what world something belongs to.

Here are some example sentences that show the range of the word:

  • "The general had a martial look about him — straight-backed, cold-eyed, and utterly calm." — Here it describes a soldier-like physical presence.
  • "The protesters were met with a martial response — armoured vehicles and armed troops filled the streets." — Here it means a response of military force.
  • "She trained in several martial disciplines before becoming a professional fighter." — Here it refers to combat-based skills.
  • "The government declared martial law after the capital fell into chaos." — Here it refers to military rule.
  • "The poem had a martial quality — every line felt like a battle cry." — Here it captures the feeling of war and combat, even in a piece of writing.

If you had to boil it down to one line:

Martial means of, relating to, or suggesting war, combat, soldiers, and the military — either in a literal sense or in spirit.

Every use of the word, no matter how varied, traces back to that core idea. Once you see the "war/soldier" connection clearly, the word will click into place naturally whenever you encounter it.
10394:
A martinet is a person in authority who demands strict, unquestioning obedience to rules and who enforces those rules with rigid, often excessive harshness — showing little or no flexibility, compassion, or common sense.

In simpler terms: a martinet is someone who is obsessed with rules and discipline to an unreasonable degree. They don't just want order — they want total control over how things are done, down to the smallest detail, and they punish any deviation, no matter how trivial.
What Exactly Makes Someone a Martinet?

Not every strict person is a martinet. A good teacher can be firm and demanding, yet still be fair and respected. What separates a martinet from a simply strict person is a specific cluster of qualities:

They follow the rules blindly. A martinet doesn't ask why a rule exists or whether it makes sense in a given situation. The rule exists, so it must be followed — end of discussion. They prioritize the letter of the rule over its spirit or purpose.

They have no flexibility. A martinet treats every situation the same way, regardless of context. A student who is late because of a genuine emergency gets the same punishment as one who was just careless. There are no exceptions, ever.

They enforce even petty, trivial rules with the same seriousness as important ones. This is a hallmark of a martinet. They will reprimand a soldier for a slightly crooked button on his uniform with the same intensity they'd use for a serious offense. Their sense of proportion is off.

They are often authoritarian and cold. A martinet typically isn't interested in your explanation, your feelings, or your circumstances. What matters to them is compliance — did you follow the rule or not?

They tend to love their own authority. Many martinets enjoy the power their position gives them. Enforcing rules is a way of asserting that power, and they take it very seriously.
The Tone of the Word — Is It a Compliment?

No, never. "Martinet" is always a criticism. It is a negative, disapproving word. When you call someone a martinet, you are saying that their strictness has gone too far — that it has become unreasonable, joyless, and even harmful. It suggests the person has lost sight of the bigger picture and has become obsessed with control for its own sake.

Nobody ever introduces themselves as a martinet. It is a label that other people put on someone to criticize them. Think of it as a polite but pointed insult.
Where Would You Encounter a Martinet?

The word is most commonly used in these settings:

In the military, a commanding officer who punishes soldiers harshly for the tiniest uniform or protocol violations, going far beyond what is necessary for discipline.

In schools, a teacher or principal who gives severe consequences for the most minor infractions — a half-inch of shirt untucked, a pencil that isn't sharpened exactly right — without any warmth or reasonableness.

In the workplace, a manager or boss who micromanages every detail, demands that all procedures be followed to the letter regardless of efficiency, and reprimands employees for the most minor deviations.

In a family setting, a parent who runs the household like a military camp, demanding perfect obedience and punishing children for the smallest mistakes.

"The new army colonel was a total martinet — soldiers were punished for failing to polish the backs of their belt buckles, which no one ever even saw."

"Mr. Henderson was such a martinet that he once gave a student a zero for writing her name one centimeter too low on the page."

"Working under a martinet is exhausting — you spend more energy worrying about tiny formalities than actually doing your job well."

"She wasn't just strict; she was a genuine martinet who enforced every single company policy with zero exceptions, even when everyone agreed a rule made no sense."
The Crucial Difference: Strict vs. Martinet

This is important, because people often confuse the two.

A strict person has high standards and enforces them consistently, but they have good judgment. They understand why rules exist, they apply them proportionally, and they are still human. You may not always like a strict person, but you can usually respect them.

A martinet has crossed a line. Their strictness is no longer in service of any real goal — it has become an end in itself. They enforce rules for the sake of enforcing rules. They confuse obedience with achievement, and control with good leadership. A martinet often actually produces worse results than a balanced leader would, because people under their command become resentful, fearful, and focused on avoiding punishment rather than doing good work.

The word "martinet," in short, is what you use when "strict" is no longer strong enough — when someone's obsession with discipline and order has slipped into something small-minded, unreasonable, and authoritarian.
10395:
A martyr is a person who suffers deeply — or even dies — for something they believe in so strongly that they refuse to give it up, even when they are threatened, punished, or persecuted for it.

The heart of the word is this: a martyr faces a choice. They can either abandon their belief and be safe, or hold on to it and pay a terrible price. A martyr always chooses to hold on — and suffers as a result. That refusal to back down, even under extreme pressure, is what makes someone a martyr.
The religious use — the most traditional meaning

The word is most powerfully and most commonly used in a religious context. A religious martyr is someone who is killed because of their faith, and who refuses to deny or abandon that faith even when death is the only alternative.

The early Christians killed by the Roman Empire are the most famous historical example. Roman authorities sometimes gave them an easy way out: just deny your faith, worship the Roman gods, and you will go free. Those who refused and were executed as a result became honored as martyrs. They are deeply revered in Christianity — many are recognized as saints. The same concept exists in Islam, where a person who dies defending their faith is called a martyr (shaheed in Arabic), and in other religions as well.

The key is always the same: the person could have survived by giving up their belief, but they chose not to.
The broader use — political and social martyrs

Over time, the word expanded beyond religion. It is now also used for people who suffer or die for any deeply held cause — a political belief, a struggle for justice, a fight for freedom or human rights.

If a person is imprisoned, tortured, or killed by a government for standing up for their people or their principles — and they refuse to compromise those principles even to save themselves — they can be called a martyr. Many figures from history who were executed or assassinated for challenging unjust systems are remembered and honored as martyrs by those who believed in their cause.
An important nuance: the label is not neutral

Whether someone is called a martyr almost always depends on who is doing the labeling. One group's martyr is often another group's criminal, traitor, or extremist. The word carries enormous emotional power — calling someone a martyr is a way of declaring that their suffering was meaningful, noble, and worthy of honor. This is exactly why the word is so frequently disputed in politics and religion. Both sides in a conflict may call their own dead martyrs, while calling the other side's dead criminals. The word, in this sense, is not just descriptive — it is also a form of tribute and legitimacy.
The everyday, informal use — "Stop being a martyr"

In ordinary conversation, the word takes on a lighter, more critical edge. In this everyday sense, a martyr is someone who constantly complains about how much they suffer, or who makes unnecessary sacrifices and then ensures everyone around them knows about it — in order to win sympathy, admiration, or guilt from others.

For example, imagine a colleague who stays late at the office without being asked, and then says with a heavy sigh, "I worked until midnight again... but I suppose someone had to do it." If they keep doing this and drawing attention to their suffering, others might say, "Don't be such a martyr." The message is: stop performing your suffering to make others feel sorry for you or grateful to you.

This informal use is quite different in tone from the serious one — it is gently mocking or critical, suggesting that the person is exaggerating or fishing for attention rather than genuinely enduring something noble. Context always tells you which sense of the word is meant: serious and honored, or informal and slightly sarcastic.

Closely related to the informal use is the phrase martyr complex, which describes a recurring psychological pattern. A person with a martyr complex habitually takes on unnecessary burdens, suffers loudly (or pointedly quietly), and positions themselves as the long-suffering, self-sacrificing hero of every situation. Their identity becomes built around being the one who gives the most and suffers the most. This is less about genuine sacrifice and more about how the person sees themselves and wants others to see them.

The noun martyrdom refers to the experience, act, or condition of being a martyr — the suffering, persecution, or death that a martyr endures. You might say someone "died in martyrdom" (meaning they died for their belief without renouncing it), or that "the history of the church is filled with stories of martyrdom."

A martyr is someone who holds on to what they believe — whether a religious faith, a political cause, or a moral principle — at the cost of great suffering or even their life. In its serious form, it is one of the most honorable titles a person can be given, suggesting extraordinary courage and conviction. In its casual form, it gently criticizes someone who is being theatrical about their suffering. The word you are reading and the tone of the conversation around it will almost always make it clear which meaning is in play.
10396: Martyrdom is the suffering or death that a person willingly accepts rather than give up something they deeply believe in — a faith, a cause, a truth, or a principle. It is not just any suffering. It is suffering that comes as a price for refusing to abandon what you stand for.

Imagine someone tells you: "Deny what you believe, or we will hurt you — or even kill you." A person who says "No, I will not deny it, even if it costs me everything" — and then faces the consequences — is experiencing martyrdom.

The word always carries two essential ingredients. First, a choice: the person could have escaped the suffering by giving in, but they chose not to. Second, a cause greater than themselves: they are not suffering for personal gain, but for a belief, a religion, a people, or a principle they hold sacred.

This is why martyrdom is almost always spoken of with a sense of deep respect, even awe. It represents the highest possible commitment a person can show to something — the willingness to pay with their own body or life.

Martyrdom finds its most powerful and classic use in religious history. In early Christianity, thousands of believers were tortured and killed by Roman authorities who demanded they renounce their faith. Those who refused and died for their belief were called martyrs, and what they underwent was called martyrdom. The same concept exists in Islam, where dying in defense of one's faith is considered a form of martyrdom, and in Judaism, Sikhism, and many other traditions.

In religious contexts, martyrdom is often seen not just as tragedy, but as the ultimate act of devotion — proof that one's faith is absolutely real and unshakeable.

Over time, the word expanded beyond religion. Anyone who suffers greatly or dies for a powerful cause — political freedom, justice, human rights — can be said to have met martyrdom. Think of political activists who are imprisoned, tortured, or executed by oppressive governments for speaking the truth or fighting for their people. Their suffering is also called martyrdom. Their legacy often becomes a rallying point for others, because martyrdom has a way of amplifying a cause rather than silencing it. A government that kills a martyr often discovers it has only made the cause stronger.

English also uses "martyrdom" in a lighter, more ironic, even slightly humorous way in everyday life. Here, it describes someone who exaggerates their suffering or constantly presents themselves as a victim in order to gain sympathy or attention. If your friend sighs dramatically every time they wash the dishes and talks about how exhausted and unappreciated they are, you might say they are treating dishwashing as an act of martyrdom. This usage is affectionate but gently mocking — it borrows the heaviness of the original word to highlight how someone is overdoing their complaints.

This is connected to what people call a martyr complex — a pattern where someone seems to seek out suffering or enjoy feeling like a victim, often because it earns them sympathy or a sense of moral superiority over others.
The emotional weight of the word

The word martyrdom carries a very particular emotional gravity. It is not neutral. When used seriously, it evokes sacrifice, courage, grief, and often — inspiration. Martyrs tend to become symbols. Their stories are told for generations. Their deaths are remembered not as defeats, but as proof that an idea was worth dying for.

When used ironically (in the everyday sense), it gently deflates someone's self-pity by comparing their mild inconvenience to something genuinely monumental.
Putting it all together with examples

"The saint's martyrdom inspired thousands to keep the faith alive even under persecution." — Here it means death for religious belief.

"Her martyrdom in the fight for civil rights turned her into a symbol that outlived her oppressors." — Here it means suffering and death for a political cause.

"He described mowing the lawn with such martyrdom that you'd think he'd crossed a desert." — Here it is used ironically to describe exaggerated suffering.
One-line summary to anchor it all

Martyrdom is the state of willingly enduring great suffering or death for a belief or cause you refuse to abandon — and in everyday speech, it can also mean the dramatic performance of suffering to win sympathy.
10397:
To marvel means to feel a deep, almost overwhelming sense of wonder or amazement at something — usually because it seems extraordinary, beautiful, impressive, or almost too good or strange to be real.

It is not just noticing that something is good or interesting. It is being struck by something so powerfully that you feel a kind of inner stillness or awe. Think of the moment you first see something breathtaking — a mountain range, a piece of music that gives you chills, a person doing something seemingly impossible. That feeling of being captivated, almost speechless, is what "marveling" captures.

When you marvel at something, two things are happening at once:

  1. You are recognizing that something is extraordinary — beyond the ordinary, beyond what you expected.
  2. You are emotionally moved by it — it is not a cold, logical observation. There is a warmth to it, a sense of being genuinely affected.

This is why "marvel" feels richer than simply saying "I noticed" or even "I was impressed." Marveling is what happens when the mind and the heart both respond at the same time.

The most important patterns to know:

1. Marvel + at + something
This is the most common structure. You marvel at a thing, a person, or a situation.

  • She stood at the window and marveled at the snowstorm.
  • He marveled at the old man's memory — he could recall every detail from sixty years ago.
  • The tourists marveled at the cathedral's ceiling.

2. Marvel + that + (full sentence)
You use this when what amazes you is a fact or a situation.

  • I marvel that she remains so patient after everything she has been through.
  • They marveled that a child so young could speak three languages.

3. Marvel + how + (full sentence)
This is used when what amazes you is the way something happens or the degree to which something is true.

  • We marveled at how quietly the engine ran.
  • I often marvel at how quickly time passes.

4. Marvel alone, without an object
Sometimes you just use it to describe the act of being in awe, without specifying what caused it.

  • We walked through the ancient ruins and could only marvel.
  • She looked up at the night sky and marveled.
The Register: When Do People Use This Word?

"Marvel" as a verb is slightly more formal and literary than everyday words like "be amazed" or "be blown away." You will find it often in writing — novels, essays, journalism — and in reflective, thoughtful speech. That said, it is not stiff or old-fashioned. It fits naturally in conversation when someone is being a little more deliberate or expressive.

It is also a timeless word, not tied to any trend or generation.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding what makes "marvel" different from nearby words is one of the best ways to truly own it.

Marvel vs. Wonder (verb)
These are very close, and often interchangeable. But "wonder" has a second meaning — to ask yourself a question, to be curious about something ("I wonder what she meant"). Marvel does not carry that meaning at all. Marvel is purely about awe and amazement. If you want to express pure, undiluted wonder, "marvel" is the cleaner choice.

Marvel vs. Admire
To admire something means to think highly of it, to appreciate its qualities. Admiration is composed and evaluative — you step back and judge something to be good. Marveling is less composed. It is more visceral, more of an involuntary response. You choose to admire; you are stopped in your tracks when you marvel.

Marvel vs. Be amazed
"Amazed" leans more toward surprise — something caught you off guard. Marvel leans more toward awe — the thing is extraordinary in a way that makes you feel small or humbled, even if you expected it. You can marvel at something you have seen a hundred times (a sunrise, a master musician's performance), precisely because marveling is not about surprise. It is about the depth of your response.

Marvel vs. Be astonished / Be astounded
These words are stronger on the disbelief side — something so unexpected it is hard to process. Marvel is more graceful, more reverent. It does not require disbelief, only a deep sense of awe.

Marvel can also be used ironically or sarcastically, usually to express disbelief or exasperation at something negative.

  • I marvel at his ability to say exactly the wrong thing every single time.
  • She marveled at how thoroughly he had managed to ignore her instructions.

Here, the speaker is not genuinely filled with awe. They are using the language of awe to highlight how absurd or frustrating something is. The context and tone make the irony clear. This is a common and very natural use — just be aware of it so you are not confused when you encounter it.

It helps to think of marvel as sitting near the top of a scale of positive emotional responses:

Like → Appreciate → Admire → Be impressed → Be amazed → Marvel / Be in awe

Marveling is close to the peak. It is not something you feel about ordinary things. It is reserved for the genuinely extraordinary — or, in the ironic case, the extraordinarily bad.

• Scientists continue to marvel at the complexity of the human brain.
  • As a child, I would marvel at how my grandmother could make a full meal out of almost nothing.
  • The audience marveled at the tightrope walker's calm as he crossed the gorge.
  • Centuries later, historians still marvel that the bridge was built without any modern machinery.
  • I sat quietly and marveled — there are simply no other words for what I felt.
To marvel is to feel a deep, reverential sense of wonder and amazement at something extraordinary — to be so struck by it that you pause, emotionally moved, and take it in fully.
10398:
Marvelous describes something that is extraordinarily good, impressive, or wonderful — so good that it fills you with a sense of wonder or delight. It goes far beyond "nice" or "good." When you call something marvelous, you are saying it is genuinely remarkable and left a strong positive impression on you.

Think of it this way: if "good" is a 6/10 and "great" is an 8/10, then marvelous is closer to a 10/10. It is a word of genuine admiration and enthusiasm.
The two layers of meaning

Marvelous carries two closely related ideas, and both are active in how the word is used:

1. Something that causes wonder or amazement
This is the deeper sense. Something marvelous is so extraordinary that it makes you stop and think, "How is this even possible?" It triggers a feeling of awe. For example, the way a spider builds a perfectly symmetrical web, or how a symphony orchestra creates a wave of emotion out of thin air — these can be called marvelous because they inspire a kind of wonder.

2. Something simply excellent or very pleasing
In everyday use, marvelous is also used to express that something is thoroughly enjoyable or very good, without necessarily inspiring deep awe. "We had a marvelous evening" just means the evening was truly wonderful and enjoyable. This is the more common, casual use.

Both meanings live in the same word. Context tells you which one is stronger in a given sentence.
The feeling it carries

When you use marvelous, you are not being neutral. The word carries genuine enthusiasm and warmth. It signals that the speaker is genuinely impressed or delighted — not just politely saying something is fine. There is a brightness and positivity built into the word itself.

Compare:

  • "The concert was good." → polite, mild
  • "The concert was marvelous." → the speaker was truly moved by it
How strong is it compared to similar words?

Here is how marvelous sits among related words, explained plainly:

  • Good / Nice — basic approval. No strong emotion.
  • Great / Wonderful — clearly positive, warm approval.
  • Marvelous — strong admiration, a sense of genuine delight or awe.
  • Magnificent / Spectacular — these often emphasize something grand in scale or visually striking (a magnificent palace, a spectacular sunset). Marvelous is broader and more personal — it can apply to a small act of kindness just as easily as a grand view.
  • Miraculous — this implies something that seems almost impossible, like a miracle. Marvelous does not go that far; it just means exceptionally impressive.
  • Extraordinary — means "beyond ordinary," and is slightly more neutral and descriptive. Marvelous is warmer and more enthusiastic.
  • Phenomenal — means exceptional to an extreme degree, often used for performance or talent. Marvelous is slightly softer and more broadly applicable.

So marvelous sits in the upper tier of positive adjectives — above "great" and "wonderful," roughly on the same level as "magnificent" and "spectacular," but warmer and more versatile than those.
What kinds of things can be marvelous?

Almost anything can be described as marvelous — experiences, achievements, people, places, events, and even ideas. Here are examples across different contexts:

  • An experience: "It was a marvelous trip through the mountains."
  • An achievement: "Landing a spacecraft on Mars is a marvelous feat of human engineering."
  • A performance: "The dancer gave a marvelous performance that left the audience speechless."
  • A person: "She has a marvelous ability to make everyone feel welcome."
  • News: "That is marvelous news — congratulations!"
  • Nature: "The way a caterpillar transforms into a butterfly is truly marvelous."
  • A meal or experience: "Dinner was absolutely marvelous."

Notice how the word fits all of these naturally, from grand achievements to simple everyday joys.
Words that reinforce it

Marvelous is often strengthened with intensifiers:

  • Absolutely marvelous — the strongest, most enthusiastic form
  • Simply marvelous — means "straightforwardly wonderful, without any doubt"
  • Quite marvelous (especially in British English) — still very positive, slightly more understated in tone
  • Truly marvelous — emphasizes sincerity
Its opposite

The antonyms of marvelous are words that describe something unremarkable, poor, or terrible:

  • Dreadful, terrible, awful — strongly negative (complete opposites)
  • Mediocre — not good, not bad, just passable
  • Ordinary, unremarkable, underwhelming — lacking any special quality

So if something fails to impress or is disappointing, marvelous is the last word you would use for it.
American vs. British English

You will see two spellings: marvelous (American English) and marvellous (British English). Both mean exactly the same thing — the only difference is the spelling convention.

In British English, marvellous is very commonly used in everyday speech as enthusiastic praise. British speakers might say "Oh, that's marvellous!" quite freely, and sometimes even lightly or ironically when something is unexpectedly good or amusing.

In American English, marvelous is used but feels slightly more expressive and literary than in British English — it carries a little more weight when an American uses it.
Tone and register

Marvelous can comfortably be used in both formal and informal settings:

  • In a formal essay or speech: "The scientist's marvelous discovery changed medicine forever."
  • In casual conversation: "Oh, that cake you made was absolutely marvelous!"

It is never out of place. However, it leans slightly more toward elegant or enthusiastic expression rather than blunt everyday speech. Someone using marvelous is usually someone who wants to convey genuine warmth and admiration, not just state a fact.
Quick mental picture

Imagine watching a street performer who, against all odds, balances twenty spinning plates while blindfolded and playing a violin with his feet. Your jaw drops. You think, "I can't believe what I just saw." That feeling — that mix of delight, surprise, and deep admiration — is exactly what the word marvelous is built to capture and express.
In one sentence
Marvelous means something is so impressively good or wonderful that it fills you with genuine delight and admiration, often to the point of wonder.
10399: Marzipan is a smooth, soft, sweet paste made from ground almonds and sugar. Think of it as edible modeling clay — sweet, nutty, and pliable enough to shape with your hands.

The two essential ingredients are finely ground almonds and sugar. These are mixed together and kneaded until the mixture comes together into a smooth, uniform paste. A small amount of egg white, honey, or rosewater is sometimes added — egg white helps bind everything, rosewater adds a subtle floral note, and honey can be used in place of some sugar.

The ratio of almonds to sugar matters a great deal. High-quality marzipan contains a high proportion of almonds — often half or more by weight — which gives it a rich, deep, nutty flavor. Cheaper versions use less almond and more sugar, or swap out some almond for less expensive ingredients, resulting in a blander, overly sweet product.
What it looks, feels, and tastes like

Fresh marzipan is pale cream or off-white in color, though it's very commonly dyed with food coloring to make it colorful.

In terms of texture, it sits somewhere between soft clay and firm dough. It is smooth, dense, and slightly moist, yet holds its shape well. When you press it, it yields and stays pressed — it doesn't spring back like bread dough. This quality is exactly what makes it so useful for shaping and sculpting.

The flavor is sweet and distinctly almondy — rich and nutty, with a slight bitterness underneath from the almonds themselves, balanced out by the sugar. It is not sharp or overwhelming; it's a gentle, rounded sweetness with a pleasant depth.

Marzipan has a wide range of uses in baking, confectionery, and decoration:

1. Covering cakes
In the UK and several European countries, marzipan is rolled out into a flat sheet and used to wrap the outside of celebration cakes — particularly Christmas cakes and wedding cakes — before a final layer of white icing (fondant) is applied on top. The marzipan layer seals the cake, adds flavor, and gives the icing a perfectly smooth surface to sit on.

2. Shaping into figures and decorations
Because it behaves like soft clay, marzipan can be sculpted into fruits, vegetables, animals, flowers, and all manner of miniature figures. These shaped pieces are then often painted with food coloring to make them look strikingly realistic. A bowl of marzipan oranges, strawberries, and bananas can be remarkably convincing. This is both a traditional craft and a fine art in many parts of Europe.

3. Eating as a sweet or candy
Marzipan is sold on its own as a confection — small blocks, logs, or shaped pieces, sometimes coated in dark or milk chocolate. These are eaten as sweets in the same way you might eat a truffle or a chocolate.

4. As a filling
It is commonly used as a filling inside chocolates, pastries, and tarts. It also appears as a filling or layer inside traditional baked goods, such as the German Christmas bread Stollen, which has a log of marzipan running through its center. Danish pastries sometimes contain an almond filling that is essentially marzipan or a close relative of it.

5. In baking generally
Small pieces or a thin layer of marzipan can be incorporated into cookies, tarts, and cakes to add a concentrated almond flavor and a slightly moist, tender texture wherever it's placed.

Marzipan has deep roots in European confectionery tradition. A few places stand out:

  • Germany — The city of Lübeck is the marzipan capital of the world. Lübecker Marzipan is a protected product with strict rules (at minimum, half its weight must be almonds). German marzipan tends to be moist, slightly grainy, and deeply flavored. It is a traditional gift at Christmas.
  • Spain — The city of Toledo is famous for its mazapán, which is drier and firmer than the German variety. It is shaped into elaborate figures and associated with Christmas.
  • Scandinavia — Marzipan is used extensively in Danish and Norwegian pastries and in prinsesstårta, a Swedish cake layered with cream and jam and covered in green marzipan.
  • Netherlands — Marzipan fruits and figures are traditional gifts for the celebration of Sinterklaas (Saint Nicholas' Day) in December.
  • UK — Marzipan appears reliably on Christmas cakes and Simnel cake, a fruit cake associated with Easter.

These two terms are sometimes used interchangeably, but they are not quite the same thing. Almond paste has a higher proportion of almonds relative to sugar, which makes it coarser, less sweet, and softer — it is more of a baking ingredient than a ready-to-eat confection. Marzipan has more sugar, is smoother, firmer, and sweeter, and is refined enough to eat on its own or use for decoration. Marzipan is essentially an elevated, more polished version of almond paste.

You may occasionally encounter something labeled marzipan that tastes slightly different or costs notably less. This could be persipan, a substitute made from ground apricot or peach kernels instead of almonds. It looks almost identical and has a similar texture, but the flavor is less rich and more bitter. It is used in lower-cost products to reduce the expense of almonds. High-quality marzipan will always clearly state almonds as the primary ingredient.

Marzipan is an almond-and-sugar paste with a smooth, pliable texture and a sweet, nutty flavor. It is eaten as a candy, used to decorate and cover cakes, sculpted into decorative figures, and baked inside pastries and breads. It has centuries of history in European confectionery, is most closely associated with Germany, Spain, and Scandinavia, and is at its finest when it contains a generous proportion of real almonds.
